services.seoDescription: Personal training at Helix Training in Corvallis — strength-based coaching from a team led by a Doctor of Physical Therapy. Movement assessment first, then a plan built for you.

faqs.q: Do I need to be in shape before I start personal training?
faqs.a: No. Personal training is where a lot of people start. We meet you where you are and build from there.

faqs.q: How often do people train one-on-one?
faqs.a: That depends on your goals and schedule. Your coach will suggest a rhythm after your first session, and many people pair personal training with group classes.

faqs.q: Can personal training help with an old injury?
faqs.a: We start every client with a movement assessment and a conversation about your history. We coach around what you can do well and refer you to a physical therapist or doctor when something needs medical care.

services.body:
Personal training at Helix is intentional, strength-based coaching built for real life and long-term, pain-free performance. Whether you're new to training, rebuilding strength, navigating a life transition, or just want smart, sustainable progress, sessions are designed around your body, your goals, and your season of life.

## What a session looks like

- **A plan with a purpose.** Programming that blends functional strength, mobility, conditioning, and skill work — nothing random.
- **Coaching, not counting reps.** Your coach watches how you move, adjusts on the spot, and explains why.
- **A movement assessment first.** Before we load anything, we look at how you move and talk through your history.
- **Practical nutrition guidance** that supports strength, resilience, and long-term health.

## Who it's for

People who want individual attention, people coming back from time off or an injury, people training for something specific, and people who simply learn better one-on-one.

## What it costs

Send us a note and we'll walk you through personal training options and pricing.

services.body:
Group strength classes are the heart of Helix. They're structured strength workouts designed to build confidence and lasting results — 60 minutes that blend strength training and conditioning into a full-body session led by an experienced coach.

## What to expect

- **A written plan, every day.** Classes follow a progressive program so you get stronger over months, not just tired for an hour.
- **Coaching at every station.** Small class sizes mean personal attention on your form.
- **Scaled to you.** Brand new or seasoned, the workout meets you where you are.
- **People who cheer for you.** You're never doing it alone. This is a community that pushes, supports, and celebrates each other.

## Who it's for

Adults of every fitness level who want to get stronger in a supportive room — whether you're brand new or experienced.

## How to start

Your first class is free. Book it, show up a few minutes early, meet your coach, and jump in.

faqs.a: For most healthy adults, yes — and it's one of the best things you can do for bone density, balance, and independence. We start slow, coach every rep, and adjust for what your body needs. Talk with your doctor first if you have a medical condition.

faqs.q: I have achy knees and a stiff back. Can I still do this?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Coaches modify movements and build gradually. If something needs medical care, we'll say so and point you to the right person.

faqs.q: Do I need to be a member to try it?

services.body:
Strength+ is a focused training program for people over 50 who want to stay strong, capable, and confident in everyday life. Sessions center on safe, progressive strength work, mobility, balance, and functional movement — whether you're brand new, coming back after a break, or already an experienced lifter.

## What to expect

- **Progressive strength work** that builds the kind of strength you use every day: getting up from the floor, carrying groceries, climbing stairs without a second thought.
- **Balance and mobility** built into every session.
- **Modifications on the spot.** Coaches adjust every movement to fit you.
- **A room full of people like you.** Encouragement, laughter, and no one watching the clock.

## What members tell us

Better strength and mobility. Better balance and confidence moving. More energy. And the thing that matters most over a lifetime: consistency, because they actually enjoy coming.

New to strength training? Start here. Strong Foundations is a 6-week introductory course that covers the fundamentals: safe lifting technique, how to feel the right muscles working, how to warm up, and how to recover. It runs in a small group with certified coaches who refine your form every week.

## Who it's for

- People new to exercise or strength training
- Anyone who wants to refresh their lifting form
- Current Helix members who want to sharpen technique or explore lift variations

Helix regulars, new lifters, and curious humans are all welcome.

## Next session

The next session is being scheduled. Email [kathy@helixtrain.com](mailto:kathy@helixtrain.com) or use the contact form and we'll let you know the moment dates are set.

articles.title: Is Strength Training Safe After 50? What I Tell New Members
articles.excerpt: Yes — for most healthy adults it's one of the best things you can do for bone, balance, and independence. Here's how we start people over 50 in Corvallis.
articles.docNotes: SEED ARTICLE — written by the setup kit as a working example. Kathy reviews, edits into her own voice, and flips draft to false to publish. Every reference link must be opened and confirmed before publishing.
articles.body:
Short answer: yes. For most healthy adults over 50, strength training is safe, and it is one of the highest-return things you can do for the next thirty years of your life. When I see someone walk into our gym in Corvallis for the first time at 58 or 67, the question underneath "is this safe?" is usually "is it too late?" It isn't. Muscle responds to training at every age we have studied.

## Why does strength matter more after 50, not less?

Because this is the decade when the body starts quietly withdrawing it. The American College of Sports Medicine's position stand on older adults (2009) lays out the pattern: muscle, strength, and bone all decline with normal aging, and an inactive lifestyle speeds every part of it up. What people notice first isn't a smaller arm — it's a harder time getting off the floor or carrying two grocery bags up the stairs.

The good news is that muscle and bone both answer to the same signal: load. The LIFTMOR trial (Watson et al., 2018) took 101 postmenopausal women, average age 65, all with low bone mass, and had half of them lift heavy twice a week for 30 minutes under supervision for eight months. Spine bone density rose 2.9% in the lifting group and fell 1.2% in the control group, every measure of physical function improved, and the researchers reported only one minor adverse event — a back spasm — in a population that, in their words, isn't usually prescribed heavy lifting because of "a perceived high risk of fracture." 

## Is it actually safe?

The injury rate for supervised strength training is low. Even in competitive weight-training sports, where the loads are far beyond anything we use with a new member, a 2017 systematic review (Keogh and Winwood, 2017) found rates from under 1 up to about 7.5 injuries per 1,000 hours of training, which the authors describe as low compared with common team sports. In our gym the numbers that matter are simpler: a coach watches every rep, the first session is an assessment rather than a workout, and we scale load to the person in front of us.

Three things make it safe in practice:

1. **Start lighter than feels necessary.** The first two weeks are about learning positions, not chasing weight.
2. **Progress in small steps.** Adding 2–5 pounds a week compounds fast. Jumping 20 pounds because it "felt easy" is how people get hurt.
3. **Respect pain that changes the movement.** Muscles working hard feel like effort. Sharp, joint-level, or radiating pain means we stop and modify.

When I coach Strength+, our over-50 class, I tell people the same thing every week: the goal is to leave feeling better than you came in, not wrecked.

## What about my knees, back, or shoulders?

Most people over 50 have something. The question isn't whether you have an achy knee; it's whether we can find movements that load the muscles around it without provoking it. Usually we can. A 2015 Cochrane review of 54 trials found that land-based exercise therapy reduced pain and improved function in people with knee osteoarthritis, with a benefit the authors described as comparable to what is "reported for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs" (Fransen et al., 2015).

That said, I'm a physical therapist, and here is where I put on that hat: if you have a recent injury, a diagnosed condition, or pain that is getting worse, see your doctor or a PT before you start. Coaching is not medical care, and a good gym knows the difference.

## How often should someone over 50 lift?

Here's my coaching answer, not a research finding: two or three sessions a week. The ACSM position stand recommends that exercise for older adults include aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and flexibility work, and closes with a line I'd put on the wall: "All older adults should engage in regular physical activity and avoid an inactive lifestyle." How many strength days that means is a judgment call; in our gym, two a week is where most people land, and a third is a bonus.

Rest matters as much as work. A day between strength sessions is the norm, and a walk on the off days is plenty.

## What does the first month look like at Helix?

- **Week 1:** A free first class. We do a short movement screen, talk through your history, and you take a scaled version of the workout.
- **Weeks 2–4:** Two classes a week. You learn the hinge, the squat, the press, the row, and the carry — the five patterns that cover most of daily life.
- **By the end of month one:** You know the movements, you know the coaches, and you have a baseline to build on.

If you want a slower on-ramp, [Strong Foundations](/programs/strong-foundations/) is a six-week beginner course that covers the same patterns one at a time. If you want a room full of people your age, [Strength+](/programs/strength-plus/) is built for you.

## The one thing I'd want you to take from this

Starting is safer than not starting. The risk of a supervised strength program is small and manageable. The risk of losing strength year over year is the thing that actually takes independence away. Come try a free class, meet a coach, and see how it feels.

## References

- Watson SL, et al., 2018. High-intensity resistance and impact training improves bone mineral density and physical function in postmenopausal women with osteopenia and osteoporosis: the LIFTMOR randomized controlled trial. [link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28975661/)
- Fransen M, et al., 2015. Exercise for osteoarthritis of the knee. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. [link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25569281/)
- American College of Sports Medicine, 2009. Position stand: Exercise and physical activity for older adults. [link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19516148/)
- Keogh JWL, Winwood PW, 2017. The epidemiology of injuries across the weight-training sports. Sports Medicine. [link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27328853/)
